summary: Explains how to handle multiple dialog usages in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). A single SIP dialog can carry several related associations, such as a call and a subscription, that have separate lifetimes but share state. The document describes the problems this causes and recommends how to process them correctly.

eli5.summary: Imagine one phone line carrying a chat and a package-tracking alert at once. Each can end at a different time, so you must keep track of which one is still going. This explains how.

subtitle: Why one SIP dialog carrying several independent associations is hard to get right, and how to avoid it.

tldr.problem: A SIP dialog can carry several associations, called dialog usages, such as a call and a subscription. They have separate life-cycles but share dialog state, and processing them correctly is not completely understood.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines dialog usages, surveys how each failure response affects a transaction, a usage or the whole dialog, covers matching requests to usages, and describes alternatives such as GRUUs and the Target-Dialog header field.
tldr.outcome: It argues that multiple usages should be avoided and that new applications should never introduce them. It is informative and normative-free.

facts.label: Safest way to refuse a usage

today: RFC 5057 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states that it makes no normative statements; its advice is to avoid multiple dialog usages.

sections.title: Dialogs, Usages and Shared State
sections.content:
Several SIP methods can establish a dialog, and each establishes an association within it known as a dialog usage. A dialog started by INVITE has an invite usage. A dialog started by SUBSCRIBE or REFER has a subscribe usage. A dialog can have up to one invite usage and arbitrarily many subscribe usages.

Multiple usages arise when a usage-creating action occurs inside an existing dialog, for example accepting a REFER or SUBSCRIBE sent inside a dialog set up by INVITE. A dialog exists from the first usage until the last is terminated.

REGISTER and PUBLISH do not create a dialog or a usage, even though some implementations have treated REGISTER as if it were in a dialog.

The state shared by all usages in a dialog is exactly: the Call-ID, the local and remote tags, the local and remote CSeq, the Route-set, the local contact, the remote target and the secure flag. Usage-specific state is not shared. For example, each subscription has its own duration.

Many SIP mechanisms, such as authentication, were designed assuming one usage per dialog, so they have mixed effects, some on the usage and some on the whole dialog.

Target refresh requests (INVITE, UPDATE, SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY and REFER) update the remote target when they succeed. Because the remote target belongs to the dialog, the change affects all usages. A refresh SUBSCRIBE with a different contact will send the peer's reINVITEs to that contact. Simultaneous target refreshes on several usages are ambiguous.
sections.eli5:
A dialog is one phone line between two people. A usage is something happening on the line, like a conversation or a news alert, and the line closes when the last one ends.

The phone line itself, such as the numbers being called, is shared. Each thing on the line has its own timer.

sections.title: Two Examples of Multiple Usages
sections.content:
In a transfer, Alice transfers a call she received from Bob to Carol. The invite usage starts with the 200 OK. Bob's REFER and NOTIFY then create a second usage, a subscription to event refer, which ends with a terminating NOTIFY. The dialog persists until BYE ends the invite usage.

In a reciprocal subscription, Alice subscribes to Bob's presence and Bob sends his own SUBSCRIBE inside that dialog. The two subscriptions have different expirations but share all dialog state. When Alice unsubscribes from Bob, Alice's side must keep the dialog because Bob's subscription is still active. The dialog ends only when the second subscription ends.
sections.eli5: On a call, you can also ask for a status update about something else. Each ends at its own time, and the call stays open until both are done.

sections.title: How Failure Responses Affect Usages
sections.content:
The memo asks what a 481 response to a NOTIFY means: does it end the subscription or the whole dialog? For responses of 400 and above, it sorts effects into three kinds. Transaction only affects only that request. Destroys usage ends the usage but not the dialog. Destroys dialog ends everything sharing it.

  • Transaction only: most codes, including 401, 403, 486, 488, 500, 503 and 603.
  • Destroys usage: 405, 480, 481, 489 and 501.
  • Destroys dialog: 404, 410, 416, 482, 483, 484, 485, 502 and 604.

The 481 response is the most ambiguous. The memo recommends that it destroy only the usage, unless it was the last one, though some implementations destroy the whole dialog. A 481 to a CANCEL affects only the CANCEL transaction.

Transaction timeouts should generally affect only the usage in which they occurred. Normal termination of one usage does not end others, and refreshing one subscription does not extend another. When refusing a new usage, 603 Decline is generally the safest response, since a wrong code can end the dialog and every usage.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, you need to know whether only one request failed, one activity ended, or the whole line has to hang up.

sections.title: Matching Requests to Usages
sections.content:
A dialog has at most one invite usage, so INVITE, UPDATE, PRACK, ACK, CANCEL, BYE and INFO belong to it. SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY and REFER requests are matched to a subscription by their Event header field.

OPTIONS, MESSAGE and requests with unknown methods belong to no usage. If they fail, they affect the dialog only through failures that destroy entire dialogs. The memo notes that RFC 3891 Replaces was meant to affect only the invite usage of the dialog it targets, but the interactions with multiple usages have not been well explored, and implementers should avoid that scenario completely.
sections.eli5: Each message is sorted to the activity it belongs to, using labels in the message. Some messages belong to none, like asking whether someone is there.

sections.title: Avoiding Multiple Usages
sections.content:
New applications must not require endpoints to build multiple usages, and endpoints should refuse a second usage outside existing scenarios. Transfer sent its REFER inside the existing dialog for three reasons. A REFER on a new dialog might not reach the right endpoint, it was unclear how to associate it with the invite usage, and out-of-dialog REFERs raised authorization concerns.

The memo's alternative uses a GRUU, a URI that reaches one specific user agent, which solves the first problem. The Target-Dialog header field (RFC 4538) names another dialog and handles the second and third. Join and Replaces can also address the first. In the sketched transfer, Bob sends a REFER to Alice's GRUU on a new Call-ID with Target-Dialog identifying the existing dialog, and Alice then INVITEs Carol with Replaces. No dialog is reused.
sections.eli5: Instead of squeezing a second job onto the same line, you start a fresh line and mention the first one so everyone knows how they are connected.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Handling multiple usages is complex and can disrupt communication if response codes are chosen carelessly. Third parties injecting unauthenticated requests or responses could exploit the ambiguities. Implementations that accept multiple usages should pay extra attention to the security considerations of RFC 3261.

A service that requires multiple usages must consider clients that do not destroy dialogs when expected. A service that disallows them must consider clients that destroy the whole dialog when only a usage should end. In the worst case, many misbehaving clients automatically creating multiple usages could induce a retry storm similar to an avalanche restart.
sections.eli5: Mixing up which activity ended can cause confusion, and a crowd of confused programs could all retry at once and overload a server.
